Report Briefing

California state law requires all cities and counties to submit a Housing Element Annual Progress Report (APR) to the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) by April 1 each year. The APR tracks the full housing production pipeline: project applications submitted, planning approvals, building permit approvals, and construction completion, as well as units demolished, rehabilitated, or converted. As such, the housing data collected through the APR provides a uniquely comprehensive snapshot of California housing production. While other datasets like the Census Building Permit Survey (BPS) also capture robust permitting trends, the APR offers a level of detail across development milestones about unit affordability and structure type that sets it apart.

It is essential for APR data to be accurate. HCD uses APR data to assess jurisdictional compliance with local Housing Element plans, track progress toward Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) targets by income category, and identify unmet housing needs. Advocates, policymakers, and researchers rely on it to evaluate statewide housing development trends and broader housing policy impacts. Since 2018, HCD has provided the APR form as an Excel template for jurisdictions to complete and submit their annual reports. Since then, the APR form has grown every year to incorporate other legislatively mandated reporting categories, from the use of density bonuses or various streamlining laws to tracking some forms of residential rehabilitation, rezoned areas, and student housing.

In 2025, HCD partnered with the UC Berkeley Possibility Lab to examine how local jurisdictions collect, manage, and report APR data. Rather than evaluating individual jurisdictions' compliance, this study identifies structural features of the APR process that may interfere with the ability of local jurisdictions to feasibly report housing data at the level of detail required. As such, our study is not an assessment of APR data accuracy, but rather focused on helping local governments do the APR.

Our findings draw from a statewide survey reaching 173 jurisdictions, as well as in-depth interviews from a stratified sample of 11 jurisdictions representing the diversity of localities within the state, and a small focus group with local California housing planners and government staff. Data collection to inform this report was conducted in three sequential phases between March and September 2025. Importantly, the survey, interviews, and focus group are limited in that they do not directly measure the empirical accuracy of jurisdictions’ APR submissions. However, when comparing the APR data to the Census BPS data, we find similar overall trends in the number of permitted units, where the direction of annual change is consistent in each dataset.

Taken as a whole, this study underscores the logistical challenges faced by local jurisdictions when preparing the APR and integrating new reporting requirements. The manual entry required to input various data points into the APR form increases the potential for human error, making it burdensome for local planners to ensure they are reporting complete and accurate data. Moreover, various data points are not consistently documented in jurisdictions’ existing administrative processes, requiring local planners to retrospectively track down information on a project-by-project basis when preparing the APR. The planners working on the APR take steps to validate their reported data to ensure accuracy. Nonetheless, mitigating the challenges identified in our study remains essential for enabling local governments to feasibly fulfill their data reporting obligations.

This report aims to support HCD in collecting high-quality housing data while reducing burdens on local governments. Given our findings, we’ve identified a range of specific recommendations for HCD to improve the APR process for all California jurisdictions. We acknowledge that some of these interventions may not be relevant to all jurisdictions across the state due to their varying sizes, resources, and capacities, and recognize that support from HCD may be more valuable for some jurisdictions than others.

The APR in its current form is still relatively new, and it is reasonable to assume the state will continue to collect data on housing production for years to come. As such, it is worthwhile for HCD to reflect on how the process is working, to correct issues that are identified, and to redirect course as appropriate. In this briefing, we outline the recommendations we provided to HCD as a result of our research. When preparing our report, we communicated our findings to HCD staff, who began taking action to implement the study’s recommendations, as summarized by HCD staff at the end of this briefing.

While our recommendations focus on potential interventions for HCD, the findings of our study have implications for the broader policymaking process in California. Each and every reporting requirement in the APR form is mandated by state legislation. The California Legislature requires HCD to oversee local compliance with reporting obligations, but the Legislature lacks meaningful insight into whether local governments are equipped to fulfill this function. In other words, the feedback loop is broken. How might California’s system for accelerating and tracking housing progress look different if it were co-designed with the people involved in its implementation? We offer this question as food for thought to all participants in California policymaking.

Recommendations to HCD

1. Suggested Changes to HCD’s APR Team Processes

If HCD is going to hold jurisdictions accountable for inadequate APR submissions, the department should ensure it is helping set up local governments for success. Specifically, HCD should develop and provide assistance to local governments to help them track and manage housing development data that will be reported in the APR. Jurisdictions, especially those with fewer resources, would benefit from the additional support, and HCD could better equip jurisdictions to collect and report accurate data consistent with the department’s standards.

1a. Provide guidance to clarify common points of confusion

There are certain project types and unique situations that jurisdictions struggle to report in the APR and about which HCD could provide more clarity. Specifically, planners communicated that it is not clear how they should report project amendments in the APR or precisely how to handle large master-planned developments that ultimately have many housing units and multiple buildings. In both cases, planners seem to have rightfully concluded that the APR format was not set up with these circumstances in mind. HCD staff could issue guidance to jurisdictions about how best to report on these kinds of circumstances in the APR.

1b. Provide APR instructions and guidance in more and varied formats

The role of preparing the APR frequently shifts among local government staff members. More than 20% of survey respondents, all of whom worked on the 2024 APR, reported that this was the first year they had done so. HCD’s APR Instructions and Frequently Asked Questions documents are helpful to local government staff but still insufficient. By defining terms and explaining all fields in the submission form, the existing resources help users navigate the APR, which is otherwise unintuitive for many. That said, we heard from planners who identify as more visual or auditory learners that the written instructions are not the most useful to them, and several interviewees specifically mentioned that they would benefit from instructions in the form of a video.

HCD should record and post additional videos related to specific APR topics. HCD already holds information sessions and webinars about the APR, and there is demand for this content: 56% of survey respondents attended one of these events in late 2024 or early 2025. Creating additional how-to videos may have the effect of reducing the number of questions sent to the APR inbox, thus reducing staff time spent responding to individual emails.

1c. Communicate any new APR requirements at the start of the reporting year and provide technical assistance for implementation

Local governments are constantly generating data on project applications submitted, planning approvals, and building permit approvals as housing projects move through the development pipeline. This data is stored in jurisdictions’ permit tracking systems, which are often deliberately set up to be conducive for preparing the APR, such as by including fields to collect all of the required data.

When the APR form changes from year to year, local governments must adapt to meet the new requirements. Even if the changes are relatively minor, it is possible (and even likely) that local governments have not been collecting data in that format or collecting that information at all during the reporting year. Interviewees expressed frustration about being made aware of changes to the APR near the end of the reporting year, especially if the change requires them to track down pieces of information they had not been recording for projects. A late adjustment to the APR creates more work for local government staff in the few months before the APR is due, which is already a period of overwork for many of the people tasked with preparing APRs.

Ideally, jurisdictions would be informed of any changes to the APR form at least a year in advance so they can appropriately adjust their data collection and storage throughout the reporting year. As an example, this might entail modifying their local application forms so project applicants submit certain pieces of information required for the APR at the outset. Some planners we spoke with feel that they are always updating their data systems and procedures because the APR regularly changes. This is especially challenging because making systematic changes can be a slow, gradual process, and local governments may plan for them months or years in advance.

1d. Provide guidance, including “plug-and-play” templates, for the most common permit tracking software systems used by jurisdictions

Among survey respondents, 87.3% reported that their jurisdiction uses some kind of “gov tech” software to track housing projects across development milestones and collect data from applications, planning approvals, building permit approvals, and construction completion. However, many jurisdictions are extracting APR data from software systems that were not specifically designed to produce it.

Software systems designed for permit tracking can be customized to varying degrees, from modifying what fields are included and designing report templates, to integration with other systems. For completing the Housing Element APR, this means that the software collects all of the required data or exports data in a structure that is conducive for transferring to the APR submission form.

Many of the commercial permit software systems allow for some amount of customization of the fields, settings, and data exports. This includes creating “templates” for reports or exporting data from the software. As long as the APR uses a spreadsheet format, how jurisdictions transfer data from their permit software to a spreadsheet format will remain a significant part of the APR preparation process. Some jurisdictions have identified “translating” their data into the APR format as a roadblock in the process and have adjusted their permit software to the extent possible, designing templates that include the specific pieces of information required for the APR and in a similar format.

Currently, jurisdictions must all individually prepare these templates and figure out the customization settings on their own, but HCD could ease the burden on local governments by providing guidance or even developing templates themselves for the most common software systems identified in our survey.

1e. Clearly establish the goals and purpose of the APR, especially as HCD’s authority for overseeing the process grows

Through interviews and our focus group, it became clear that many planners who work on the APR are not aware of or misunderstand why every city and county in California is required to complete the APR. Comments from several planners suggested they view the APR as something HCD simply forces them to do, without realizing that the requirements are legislatively mandated or that the data provide uniquely comprehensive insights into housing development across the state in a way that no other publicly accessible dataset does. This misunderstanding may lead some local staff to question the necessity of certain details — highlighting the importance of clear guidance to support consistent and confident reporting. Planners who are less aware of the APR’s goals and purposes may not view the APR as important to their work and thus be less intrinsically motivated to work on it.

In all of its messaging about the APR, HCD should include a brief explanation of why local governments must collect and submit housing production data each year. This could include a brief overview of the history and goals of the APR at the beginning of videos and webinars, as well as in written instructions or guides to preparing the APR. HCD might also explain why the accuracy of specific data points is important for policymaking or evaluation.

Particularly as HCD explores its expanded authority to reject APRs that do not substantially meet requirements through Assembly Bill (AB) 2653 (Chapter 657, Statutes of 2022), HCD could develop new technical assistance materials, such as review standards for the APR form and process, to help jurisdictions clearly understand why they may be subject to additional scrutiny when an APR is rejected or when HCD asks for revisions after submission.1

2. Suggested Changes to the APR Form

One finding that arose from nearly all of our interviews and in many survey responses is that the Microsoft Excel APR submission form is challenging to use. When asked about the biggest challenges to submitting complete and accurate APR data, the most common response was the design of the APR submission form itself, which 21% of survey respondents mentioned unprompted.

2a. Change elements of the APR submission form to make it easier to input data

Planners expressed frustration that there are built-in limitations on what users can do, such as not being able to filter data, sort columns, or copy-and-paste rows of data. Making systematic changes to the APR form that allow for more flexibility is within HCD’s “form authority” and has the potential to save significant staff time.2 A revised form might lift some of the less necessary programmed limitations or macros, such as by allowing users to paste rows of data into the tables. This change could limit frustration and reduce the amount of time planners spend working on data entry for the APR. One interviewee memorably described their experience “fighting with the macros.” Given the challenges reported in our data, HCD might consider reassessing if the negative impacts of programmed elements outweigh the intended benefits.

We also acknowledge that HCD has taken measures to make the APR form easier for local government staff to use and complete. Specifically, the workbook is programmed to automatically run most calculations and to auto-populate some fields and tables. These components of the workbook’s programming help ease the burden on planners and may reduce the amount of time spent preparing the APR submission.

2b. Consider alternative formats for collecting project-level data across development milestones

Interview and focus group participants described difficulties linking data when completing Table A2 of the APR form, where jurisdictions report on planning approvals, building permit approvals, and construction completion. Planners from large jurisdictions said linking this data was one of the most time-consuming and tedious parts of the APR. Given this, HCD might consider alternative formats for collecting project-level data across development milestones.

Though the APR submission form has been constructed to include fields for all of the required information and is intended to be suitable for most projects, interviewees felt that the current system is still not well-suited to reporting certain kinds of information. In particular, interviewees note that the current APR form is not set up to easily track large developments that begin with one large lot and result in hundreds or even thousands of new housing units across multiple subdivisions. These “family-tree” developments can be more difficult to report in the APR, as compared to those that follow a more linear project pathway.

Likewise, a few interviewees reported that it can be difficult to document project amendments in the APR form. Some planners worried about incorrectly reporting units twice (“double-dipping”) or confusing the development timeline when they needed to report a project amendment, such as its number of units or the composition of units by income level. Notably, HCD staff who work on APRs have similarly mentioned that there are instances when it is unclear how jurisdictions should report certain kinds of amendments to project milestones that have already been reported in a previous APR.3

Interviewees described how tracking a project as it moves through the development pipeline—by linking the project’s planning approvals, building permits, and construction completion—can create opportunities for errors or duplicates to emerge in Table A2. Compounding this challenge, projects often reach these milestones in different years and thus should appear in multiple years’ APRs, potentially making it more difficult to identify errors.

3. Suggested Changes to the Broader APR Process

3a. Require and support a shift toward assigning unique project identifiers

Linking project-level data across development milestones is one of the most persistent challenges planners face. In some cases, jurisdictions may not consistently assign a unique identifier to a given project as it progresses through the development phases, which can obscure linkages between project data across different documentation sources. Our findings suggest that the underlying documentation processes are a potential root cause of the difficulties faced when collecting and reporting accurate APR data, particularly for Tables A and A2.

One of the potential benefits of technology solutions is to more easily enable linking of all records for the same project, but tech solutions are only as good as their underlying documentation sources. Hypothetically, a unique project identifier could be reported in the APR as the “Local Jurisdiction Tracking ID,” thus resolving the shortcomings of APNs for linking project-level data across milestones. By our own observation, though, the local application materials used by jurisdictions in their development processes do not consistently assign each project a unique project identifier that is recorded across each development milestone.

For jurisdictions that do not yet have this, HCD might work with local staff to set up a system where every project has a unique project identifier that is generated when an application is received and then attached to the project until its completion, which could make it easier for local government staff to track projects over time. If pursued, this intervention would be most effective if overseen by internal HCD staff (rather than consultants) to ensure alignment with existing systems and continued support moving forward. While likely requiring substantial resources and time on the part of HCD, this intervention could nonetheless help address the challenges that local staff face when preparing the APR via the existing submission method, thus potentially mitigating wholesale changes to the Excel form and reducing the need for APR staff capacity to troubleshoot form challenges.

3b. Improve primary source documentation of affordability data for deed-restricted units

Assigning unique project identifiers could help ensure robust linkages between development milestones. However, in light of the APR requirements in Tables A and A2 for reporting unit-level affordability, it would also be helpful if a jurisdiction’s primary source documentation consistently recorded information about affordability, particularly for deed-restricted units where affordability commitments are typically formalized prior to the issuance of the building permit (if not before).

To support jurisdictions, HCD could offer templates for primary source materials (e.g., sample application forms) that jurisdictions could modify and adapt to their unique context, thus easing the burden of form design on jurisdictions and providing a clear course of action for planners pursuing this kind of improvement. If pursuing this kind of intervention, HCD should keep in mind the variation across jurisdictions, and potentially develop a suite of application material templates that would be appropriate for different configurations of local governance.

For example, HCD might provide one package that would be useful in jurisdictions where legal milestones (e.g., deed restrictions formalizing affordability commitments) and development milestones (e.g., the issuance of building permits) are overseen by different departments, and another package that would be sufficient where the governance of legal and development milestones is less fragmented. By incorporating these features into their primary source documentation across the project lifecycle, jurisdictions would be better positioned to continuously update their tracking systems with relevant APR information in real-time, as both legal and development milestones are administered.

While this intervention would likewise require effort on the part of internal HCD staff to accomplish (rather than consultants), the long-term benefits of improving on-the-ground data collection practices through consistent documentation of unit-level affordability data may be worth the initial investment of time and resources.

3c. Provide guidance and training related to affordability determinations for non-deed-restricted units

The two types of affordable housing units reported on in the APR—deed-restricted and non-deed restricted—have different challenges in terms of collecting and reporting data. Collecting affordability data for non-deed-restricted units is inherently difficult prior to construction completion, as rent levels remain responsive to market conditions that can fluctuate throughout the development lifecycle.

Throughout the housing development process, planning departments are not always aware of the price at which completed units are being rented or sold. HCD requires jurisdictions to report units without a deed restriction as above moderate-income, unless the jurisdiction provides an affordability justification as part of their APR submission.

While many jurisdictions in California can reasonably assume that any new, non-deed-restricted housing is affordable only to above moderate-income households, some smaller, more rural jurisdictions could potentially have new units on the market with rental or sales prices affordable to moderate-income households or below. Identifying non-deed-restricted (naturally occurring) affordable housing units for the APR is an additional burden on local government staff in the jurisdictions where that kind of housing exists, particularly for jurisdictions with non-deed-restricted housing that is affordable to lower-income households. A jurisdiction’s determination for streamlined ministerial approval under SB 423 (Chapter 778, Statutes of 2023) is based on its lower-income RHNA progress and its overall RHNA progress. In order to provide accurate APR data and receive credit toward their lower-income RHNA goals, those jurisdictions may be obligated to do additional fact-finding; however, absent an affordability justification, jurisdictions can always report new non-deed-restricted units as affordable to households with above moderate-incomes, which count toward overall RHNA progress.

Because developers are not typically obligated to lock in or report final rent levels for these units to local governments, APR reporting for this category relies heavily on estimation. Given that such data is often derived from observable characteristics (such as unit size and market location), this raises the possibility that HCD could estimate these values centrally, or at least provide more in-depth resources and guidance to help jurisdictions easily make those estimations on their own.

3d. Consider collecting APR data through updated technological approaches

The potential value of HCD changing the APR submission method is likely dependent on resolving observed challenges regarding on-the-ground data collection practices. Nonetheless, 19 planners in our study expressed a desire for a web- or cloud-based system to submit APR data more directly and easily. One potential approach could involve a streamlined submission method using an application programming interface (API) that integrates with multiple different permitting software programs to pull APR data directly from jurisdictions’ existing permit tracking systems. Transitioning to a new system along these lines could be a multi-year process that requires significant investment and coordination, so this recommendation should be considered as a long-term goal.

If pursued, these changes could meaningfully streamline the APR process across the board. However, if the data collection challenges observed in our study are not resolved, then the greater ease enabled by alternative methods for APR submission will only partially mitigate the level of burden placed on local jurisdictions to report accurate data.

If pursuing alternative submission models, HCD should also anticipate associated limitations, especially for low-capacity jurisdictions that lack capable software systems and have minimal ability to procure them. Yet while alternative methods for APR submission would not necessarily benefit jurisdictions with limited capacity for software improvements, HCD could still incorporate alternative methods, such that jurisdictions have multiple options for how they submit their APRs. Higher capacity jurisdictions could take advantage of an alternative submission model, while lower capacity jurisdictions could continue submitting via an APR form.

HCD Actions Pursuant to the Recommendations

When preparing this report, the Possibility Lab communicated our findings to HCD staff, who began taking action to implement the study’s recommendations, as summarized by HCD staff below.

Actions Already Implemented

  • Recommendation 1b

    • To respond to this recommendation, HCD supplemented its guidance offered through instructional documents, APR webinars, and regular 1-on-1 technical assistance to jurisdictions. The department also created new monthly office hours, open to all planning staff working on APRs. Three office hours sessions were attended by over 100 jurisdiction staff members and were met with positive feedback.

  • Recommendation 1c

    • In accordance with this desire for advanced communication about new legislative reporting requirements being added to the APR in the upcoming reporting year, HCD has sent out an advisory memo in advance of the release of 2026 APR form materials detailing what information is needed to complete the new requirements of the upcoming form. This advanced memo in 2026 will be released even earlier in future reporting years and will be designed to provide jurisdictions more time prior to reporting to understand and compile any new data that is needed for inclusion on the upcoming APR.

  • Recommendation 1e

    • Throughout the 2025 APR reporting period, HCD prioritized communication of the ultimate goals and importance of reporting high-quality APR data through its webinars, e-blasts, and individualized technical assistance communications with jurisdictions. These communications included (1) highlighting the value of APRs as critical components of a unique statewide housing dataset that facilitates opportunities for all stakeholders to study and understand the state of housing in California, as well as (2) emphasizing the administrative use of APR data by the State to determine designations for the Streamlined Ministerial Approval Process program (SMAP) and track progress toward Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) goals.

Actions In Progress

  • Recommendation 1b

    • Moving into the 2026 APR reporting period, HCD is in the process of developing a series of short instructional videos for planners that will provide further targeted guidance on both the introductory and complex topics critical to APR reporting. Among the many topics covered in these videos will be more clear guidance on how to report the family tree-style projects mentioned by planners and covered in recommendation 1a of the report.

  • Recommendation 1d

    • HCD’s APR team has engaged in preliminary discussions with the department’s Information Technology Branch about the possibility of developing templates for converting permitting data from commonly used software systems into a format which can be processed for the APR.

  • Recommendation 2a

    • For the 2026 reporting year, HCD will add filtering and sorting functions into the form – especially on the denser data tables like Table A and A2 – to increase the usability of the form and the ease with which jurisdictions can enter and keep track of their data.

    • HCD will also update its instructional documents and create an instructional video to better clarify how jurisdictions may copy and paste cells or freeze columns and rows in the form to fit their needs.

  • Recommendation 3c

    • HCD is working to address the challenges jurisdictions currently face in reporting the affordability of non-deed-restricted developments on the APR prior to the 2026 reporting period. HCD is working to provide (1) more clear guidance around what data and methods are required to justify a non-deed-restricted unit as affordable to moderate- or lower-income households, and (2) more resources for jurisdictions to use to help gather this required data.

  • Recommendation 3d

    • HCD also sees the benefits of migrating the APR data collection process to an integrated web form and has begun preliminary discussions with its IT Branch to outline what this transition would require over the coming years.
